title: The Therapeutic Gospel
subtitle: What happens when a crucified Lord is quietly traded for a God who exists to make me feel better.
question: Have we exchanged the God who calls us to die and rise for a God whose only job is to keep us calm, affirmed, and emotionally comfortable?
whyItMatters: Most of us did not decide to abandon the gospel. We softened it one Sunday at a time, until the faith we inherited became a faith that asks nothing of us and promises to settle our nerves. Sociologist Christian Smith named it moralistic therapeutic deism, the working creed of a generation that believes God wants us to be nice, to feel good about ourselves, and to stay mostly out of the way until we need help. It is not heresy shouted from a pulpit. It is heresy whispered in the assumptions, in the worship songs that never mention sin, in the prayers that ask for relief and never for repentance. I have preached it without meaning to. I have wanted my people comforted more than I have wanted them converted.
biblicalFoundation:
Jesus did not open his invitation with a promise of wellness. He said that anyone who would come after him must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow. The cross was not a metaphor for inconvenience. It was an instrument of execution, and he handed it to the people he loved most. A faith that has lost the cross has lost the thing Jesus put at the center of his call. He spoke of a narrow road and a hard gate, and he said that few find it, while the wide and easy way leads somewhere we do not want to go. The therapeutic gospel widens the gate until everyone fits and nothing is required.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer named the trade with a precision that still cuts. He called it cheap grace, grace we bestow on ourselves, grace without discipleship, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ living and incarnate. Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of the church, he wrote, because it preaches forgiveness without repentance and comfort without surrender. He paid for that conviction with his life on a gallows in 1945. He understood that grace is free but never cheap, that it cost God the death of his Son and will cost the disciple his old self.

Jesus said that whoever would save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. This is the math the therapeutic gospel cannot do. It is built to save my life, to protect my feelings, to keep me well-adjusted and undisturbed. But the gospel does not promise to improve the self. It promises to crucify it and raise a new one. Peter, writing to a frightened church, did not tell them to feel better about themselves. He told them, you shall be holy, for I am holy. Holiness is not therapy. It is the slow and costly remaking of a person into the likeness of Christ.

None of this means God is indifferent to our pain. The same Lord who carried a cross also wept at a grave and gathered children and broke bread with the broken. He heals. He comforts. But he heals by killing the old self and raising a new one, not by helping me stay comfortable as I am. The call of Christ, Bonhoeffer wrote, bids a man come and die. And on the far side of that death, only there, is the life that no therapy can give.

churchRecord.led: At its best the church has refused to let suffering have the last word. It built hospitals, sat with the dying, named grief honestly, and offered a comfort the world could not counterfeit because it was anchored in a God who suffered. The pastoral tradition from the Psalms to Eugene Peterson has insisted that God meets us in the dark, that lament is prayer, and that the wounded are not a problem to be managed but people to be loved.
churchRecord.failed: But the church has also sold the easy version when the easy version filled seats. It has preached self-esteem and called it grace, promised health and wealth and called it faith, trimmed the cross out of the message because the cross does not market well. We made the gospel a service for the religious consumer and then wondered why our people had no spine when the cost came due. I have done my share of the trimming.

whereWeAgree: The gospel does heal. It does comfort the grieving and steady the anxious and bind up the broken, and any preaching that despises those mercies has not understood the heart of God. The disagreement is never whether the gospel comforts. It is whether comfort is all it is.
captureLeft: On one side the therapeutic gospel becomes a faith of pure affirmation, a God who only ever agrees with me, whose love is real but never holy, who would never ask me to change because changing might hurt. It is kind in the way that abandons people to themselves.
captureRight: On the other side it becomes a faith of personal blessing and best-life ambition, a God enlisted to underwrite my comfort, my prosperity, my upward arc, a divine sponsor for the life I already wanted. Both versions put the self on the throne and ask God to keep it there.
whereWeDiffer: We part from both not because we want people to suffer but because we believe the self enthroned is the self destroyed, and that the only love strong enough to save is a love willing to kill what is killing us. The cross is not the absence of comfort. It is the price of the deepest comfort there is.
theCost: To preach this is to lose the crowd that came for relief and stayed for nothing. It costs the pastor his numbers and the believer his illusions. It means telling someone who came to feel better that the road runs through a death first, and trusting that the resurrection on the far side is worth the grief of the crossing. It is easier, every single week, to offer the cheaper thing.
charge: Stop asking whether your faith makes you feel better and start asking whether it is making you holy. Find the cross you have been avoiding and pick it up. Then go and tell the truth gently to someone who has only ever been handed comfort, and stay with them while it costs.
